questions.question: Review the importance of Human Resource Management. An 1 (5 X 3 = 15 Marks) Short paragraph Questions Answer any 3 out of the 5 questions (Each carries 5 marks) Question No. Questions Learning Domains Course Outcome
questions.solution_html:
• Design a training module for staff of a human service organisation on managing organizational change
  • effectively.
  •  Title: Managing Organizational Change Effectively in Human Service Organisations.
  •  Target group: Social workers, counsellors, administrators, supervisors, programme coordinators, and
  • other HSO staff.
  •  General objective: To develop staff knowledge, attitudes, and skills for understanding, implementing
  • and sustaining organizational change.
  •  Specific objectives: Enable participants to explain organizational change, identify resistance
  • communicate effectively, solve problems, and prepare an action plan.
  •  Introduction and needs assessment: Conduct a pre-training assessment and invite staff to share their
  • experiences and concerns about organizational change.
  •  Understanding organizational change: Explain its meaning, types, causes, and stages, using examples
  • such as introducing digital case records in a hospital.
  •  Identifying resistance: Discuss fear of the unknown, lack of skills, job-security concerns, increased
  • workload, and lack of trust in management.
  •  Kotter and Schlesinger’s strategies: Explain education and communication, participation and
  • involvement, facilitation and support, negotiation and agreement, co-optation, and explicit or implicit
  • coercion.
  •  Communication and leadership: Develop active listening, empathetic communication, conflict
  • resolution, feedback, and participatory leadership skills.
  •  Training methods: Use lectures, group discussions, brainstorming, case studies, role-play, and
  • collaborative exercises.
  •  Practical case study: Ask participants to develop strategies for introducing a new electronic case
  • management system when staff members resist the change.
  •  Action planning: Each group prepares an implementation plan specifying objectives, responsibilities
  • timelines, resources, staff support, and monitoring indicators.
  •  Evaluation: Use pre-tests and post-tests, role-play observations, participant feedback, and follow-up
  • assessment after one to three months.
  •  Expected outcomes and conclusion: Improved staff confidence, reduced avoidable resistance, better
  • teamwork, effective implementation, and improved quality of services for beneficiaries.
questions.source_exam: Official Model Question Paper (FYUGP 2024
questions.final_answer: Design a training module for staff of a human service organisation on managing organizational change

  •  Needs assessment: identifies community problems, vulnerable populations, and priority areas.
  •  Planning: establishes objectives, activities, timelines, and measurable outcomes for welfare programmes.
  •  Establishes administrative structures, allocates responsibilities, and defines reporting relationships.
  •  It recruits, trains, supervises, and develops qualified personnel
  •  It motivates staff, guides implementation, and ensures that organizational activities follow established
  • objectives.

  •  Service delivery: It facilitates the delivery of pensions, child protection, healthcare, disability services
  • counselling, and elderly care.
  •  Community participation: It involves beneficiaries in identifying needs, planning interventions, and
  • assessing programme performance.
  •  Monitoring: It tracks progress, service coverage, expenditure, and compliance with programme.
  •  Evaluation: It assesses programme effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, and impact
  •  Challenges and improvement: It addresses resource shortages, administrative delays, poor coordination
  • and exclusion through training, transparency, digital support, and grievance-redressal mechanisms.

  • d) Monitoring and evaluation: They help measure progress, identify gaps, and assess whether welfare
  • programmes achieve their intended outcomes.
  • e) Accountability and improvement: They promote transparency, identify implementation barriers, and
  • support corrective action to improve services for vulnerable populations.

questions.question: Judge the accountability of national-level NGOs to their beneficiaries versus their donors.
questions.solution_html:
• a) Accountability to beneficiaries: NGOs must respond to community needs, protect beneficiaries' rights
  • provide accessible services, and encourage participation in decision-making.
  • b) Accountability to donors: They must use funds according to agreed purposes, maintain accurate financial
  • records, and submit reports on activities and expenditure.
  • c) Potential conflict: Donor priorities may differ from local needs, creating tension between funding
  • requirements and community expectations.
  • d) Balancing accountability: NGOs should involve beneficiaries in programme planning while meeting
  • legitimate donor reporting and financial requirements.
  • e) Evaluation: Accountability to both groups is essential; however, beneficiary interests, dignity, and rights
  • should remain central to the NGO's mission, within applicable legal and ethical obligations.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026
questions.final_answer: should remain central to the NGO's mission, within applicable legal and ethical obligations.

questions.question: Analyze the essential conditions for creating a valid trust Part D Essay
questions.solution_html:
• a) Settlor: A person legally competent to create the trust must establish it.
  • b) Clear intention: The settlor must demonstrate a definite intention to create a trust.
  • c) Lawful purpose: The purpose of the trust must be legal and clearly identifiable.
  • d) Trust property: There must be identifiable property or assets that form the subject matter of the trust.
  • e) Beneficiaries and trustees: The beneficiaries must be identifiable or ascertainable, where required, and
  • the trust must have a valid arrangement for holding and managing the property.

questions.question: Discuss how Social Welfare Administration helps in translating social welfare policies into programmes and services.
questions.solution_html:
•  Social Welfare Administration is the process of planning, organizing, staffing, directing, coordinating
  • budgeting, and evaluating welfare programmes.
  •  It converts government policies and social welfare objectives into practical programmes and services.
  •  Needs assessment: identifies community problems, vulnerable populations, and priority areas.
  •  Planning: establishes objectives, activities, timelines, and measurable outcomes for welfare programmes.
  •  Establishes administrative structures, allocates responsibilities, and defines reporting relationships.
  •  It recruits, trains, supervises, and develops qualified personnel
  •  It motivates staff, guides implementation, and ensures that organizational activities follow established
  • objectives.
  •  It promotes cooperation - government departments, NGOs, local bodies, and community organizations.
  •  Budgeting: It estimates costs, allocates resources, expenditure, and promotes the efficient use of funds.
  •  Service delivery: It facilitates the delivery of pensions, child protection, healthcare, disability services
  • counselling, and elderly care.
  •  Community participation: It involves beneficiaries in identifying needs, planning interventions, and
  • assessing programme performance.
  •  Monitoring: It tracks progress, service coverage, expenditure, and compliance with programme.
  •  Evaluation: It assesses programme effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, and impact
  •  Challenges and improvement: It addresses resource shortages, administrative delays, poor coordination
  • and exclusion through training, transparency, digital support, and grievance-redressal mechanisms.

questions.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of the societies Registration Act in regulating registered societies.
questions.solution_html:
•  Meaning: The Societies Registration Act, 1860, provides a legal framework for registering societies
  • formed for specified charitable, educational, scientific, literary, and other eligible purposes, subject to
  • applicable law.
  •  2. Legal recognition: Registration provides a formal legal framework for the society to operate
  • according to its governing documents.
  •  3. Formation: Individuals establish a society for a lawful purpose and comply with the applicable
  • registration requirements.
  •  4. Memorandum of Association: The memorandum specifies the society’s name, objectives, governing
  • body, and other prescribed particulars.
  •  Rules and regulations: These establish procedures for membership, meetings, elections, decision
  • making, and administration.
  •  Governing body: Office-bearers and governing-body members manage the organization according to
  • its rules and applicable legislation.
  •  Registration procedure: The founders submit the prescribed application, documents, and fees to the
  • appropriate Registrar for verification.
  •  Financial accountability: Applicable legal requirements and internal governance rules support
  • responsible financial management and documentation.
  •  Annual returns and reporting: Where required by the applicable law, societies submit governing-body
  • information, accounts, or other prescribed records.
  •  Organizational continuity: Formal governance structures help maintain activities despite changes in
  • leadership or membership.
  •  Public confidence: Proper registration and transparent governance can increase confidence among
  • beneficiaries, donors, and partner organizations.
  •  Support for social development: Registered societies contribute to education, healthcare, poverty
  • alleviation, community development, and other welfare activities.
  •  Limitations: Weak monitoring, governance disputes, inadequate records, and uneven enforcement
  • may reduce regulatory effectiveness.
  •  Suggestions for improvement: Simplified procedures, proportionate financial oversight, transparent
  • reporting, democratic governance, and staff training can improve compliance.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026
questions.final_answer: reporting, democratic governance, and staff training can improve compliance.

questions.question: Design a training module for staff of a human service organisation on managing organizational change effectively.
questions.solution_html:
• effectively.
  •  Target group: Social workers, counsellors, administrators, supervisors, programme coordinators, and
  • other HSO staff.
  •  General objective: To develop staff knowledge, attitudes, and skills for understanding, implementing
  • and sustaining organizational change.
  •  Specific objectives: Enable participants to explain organizational change, identify resistance
  • communicate effectively, solve problems, and prepare an action plan.
  •  Introduction and needs assessment: Conduct a pre-training assessment and invite staff to share their
  • experiences and concerns about organizational change.
  •  Understanding organizational change: Explain its meaning, types, causes, and stages, using examples
  • such as introducing digital case records in a hospital.
  •  Identifying resistance: Discuss fear of the unknown, lack of skills, job-security concerns, increased
  • workload, and lack of trust in management.
  •  Kotter and Schlesinger’s strategies: Explain education and communication, participation and
  • involvement, facilitation and support, negotiation and agreement, co-optation, and explicit or implicit
  • coercion.
  •  Communication and leadership: Develop active listening, empathetic communication, conflict
  • resolution, feedback, and participatory leadership skills.
  •  Training methods: Use lectures, group discussions, brainstorming, case studies, role-play, and
  • collaborative exercises.
  •  Practical case study: Ask participants to develop strategies for introducing a new electronic case
  • management system when staff members resist the change.
  •  Action planning: Each group prepares an implementation plan specifying objectives, responsibilities
  • timelines, resources, staff support, and monitoring indicators.
  •  Evaluation: Use pre-tests and post-tests, role-play observations, participant feedback, and follow-up
  • assessment after one to three months.
  •  Expected outcomes and conclusion: Improved staff confidence, reduced avoidable resistance, better
  • teamwork, effective implementation, and improved quality of services for beneficiaries.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026
